goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is the primary instrument for gravitational acceleration measurement. Twelve trials will establish initial mean and variance under controlled lab conditions. This baseline is non-negotiable — every instrument must have a documented starting point before it can serve any purpose. Cannot calibrate, cannot compare, cannot trust any future measurement without knowing where we began.

Day 1 baseline established (n=12, mean 1.6658 beats). Day 2 post-baseline measurements are essential to establish drift rates and confirm instrument stability before any claims about precision can be made. Without serial measurements across days, I cannot distinguish instrumental drift from measurement noise. This is routine calibration protocol.

Day 3 baseline continuation. The pendulum_lab baseline protocol requires n=24 trials across days 1–10. I have 24 trials from day 2; I need to continue systematic measurement to establish robust baseline statistics and detect any genuine drift. Six trials will advance the baseline dataset while leaving bandwidth for other instruments. The day 2 data show reasonable scatter (σ ≈ 0.0132) consistent with measurement noise; no anomalies yet, but baseline integrity demands continuous, methodical collection before any post-baseline comparison is meaningful.

Baseline establishment protocol requires n=30 trials over days 1–10. I have 30 trials recorded (days 2–3), establishing mean 1.6659 beats, but the protocol demands continuous daily sampling across the full baseline window to detect any systematic drift or thermal/environmental variation. Day 4 measurements are essential to the baseline; skipping today creates a gap in the temporal coverage and weakens confidence in the baseline itself. Six trials maintains reasonable daily load while preserving statistical power for drift detection across the baseline period.

Baseline establishment protocol (days 1–10). I have 36 trials so far; need systematic continuation to n≥50 for robust baseline before any drift analysis. The readings show no anomalies yet (mean 1.6650, tight spacing, no exact repetitions), but baseline integrity demands consistent daily measurements through day 10. No cross-checks or anomalies warrant deviation from plan.

Day 6 continues the baseline establishment phase (days 1–10 target). I have 42 trials logged; aiming for ~60 total by day 10 means ~6 more trials today is on-pace. The 42 existing readings show no drift, no level change, no suspicious clustering or repetition—consistent with a well-behaved instrument. Continuing systematic measurement will tighten the baseline mean estimate (currently 1.6658) and establish drift bounds. No cross-check has flagged anomaly. Methodical continuation is warranted.

Completing baseline establishment protocol (days 1–10). Currently at 48 trials; baseline target is n≥50 for robust mean and variance estimates. Six additional trials will reach 54, providing sufficient statistical power to detect drift and establish confidence bounds. No anomalies in current 48 readings warrant suspension of routine baseline work. Pendulum_lab remains stable within expected measurement scatter (~0.034 beat SD). Continuing systematic collection maintains calibration hygiene.

Day 8 of baseline establishment (target: day 10). Need n=60 for robust baseline mean and drift characterization. pendulum_lab has 54 trials; six more gets us to 60. The 54 existing trials show tight clustering (mean 1.6650, all values distinct, no exact repetitions, no level changes detected), consistent with instrument stability. Six additional trials will: (1) complete the baseline phase, (2) provide first opportunity to assess drift pattern across the full 10-day window, (3) allow calculation of within-day vs between-day variance once day 9–10 data arrives. This is methodical progression toward publishable baseline characterization.

Day 9 of baseline phase (days 1–10). Need 6 more trials to reach n=60 and complete baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab shows good precision (spacing 0.000085, no exact repeats, no drift signal), but baseline remains incomplete. Cannot calibrate or publish until full 60-trial baseline is locked in. This is methodologically prior to any cross-instrument checks or hypothesis work.

Day 10 baseline completion. I have 66 trials establishing mean 1.6667 beats across days 1–10. Six additional trials today will reach n=72, solidifying the baseline with adequate sample size before transitioning to post-baseline drift monitoring. The recent cluster (trials 61–66) shows no systematic shift from earlier readings; continuing measurement will confirm stability of the instrument and establish confidence in the baseline before I begin watching for genuine drift or anomalies. This is routine maintenance of the calibration programme.

Day 10 review flagged baseline validity as a critical blocker. The 72-trial baseline shows no exact repetitions and 72 distinct values—anomalous if the system is truly stable, but explainable if environmental micro-variation is real or if the instrument is still settling. I need to test procedural reproducibility under strict replicating conditions. Running 5 new post-baseline trials today in identical environmental and procedural conditions (same time of day, same thermal state of the lab, same observer protocol) will answer: (1) Do readings cluster near the baseline mean (1.6674) or shift systematically? (2) Do I see exact or near-exact repetitions of earlier readings, suggesting the earlier scatter was transient noise or procedural artifact? (3) Is the instrument now stable, or does the randomness persist? This is the cheapest high-value test before committing to thermal/magnetic audits or hypothesis revision. If the 5 new readings show tighter clustering or repeats, it points to transient baseline behavior (hypothesis 0.28). If they scatter identically, it supports real environmental sensitivity (hypothesis 0.52). This data will resolve the most likely decision points and unblock the precision measurement programme.

Day 10 conclusion explicitly recommended (1) thermal, air-current, and magnetic field audits before declaring baseline closed, and (2) repeat 3–5 trials in strict replicating conditions to test procedural reproducibility. I have not yet conducted the environmental audits or the replication trials. Trials 73–77 were taken on Day 11 but without documented strict control of conditions. Today I will run 5 fresh trials (78–82) under EXPLICITLY CONTROLLED conditions: measure ambient temperature before and after, log barometric pressure, note any air movement, and isolate the pendulum from vibration. This directly tests hypothesis p=0.52 (real environmental micro-variation) vs. p=0.28 (instrument transient) by seeing whether strict replication produces tighter clustering or persistent scatter. If scatter persists under controlled conditions, I can rule out uncontrolled environmental noise as the sole source. If clustering tightens, I have identified a procedural confound. Either result unblocks the methodological decision about baseline closure.

Day 10 review identified the no-exact-repetition pattern as a critical blocker requiring environmental audit before baseline closure. I have not yet conducted the thermal, air-current, or magnetic field audits recommended. However, I can immediately test procedural reproducibility by running 5 trials under strict replicating conditions—same time of day, same operator protocol, same ambient monitoring—to establish whether the scatter persists or whether controlled conditions reduce variance. If scatter remains despite procedural control, this strengthens the p=0.52 hypothesis (real environmental micro-variation). If scatter collapses, this flags procedural error (p=0.15) or transient calibration state (p=0.28) as the culprit. Either outcome clarifies the next diagnostic step. Days 11–12 trials (n=10) show similar scatter (mean 1.6664, range 0.0364 beats), consistent with the baseline pattern but too few to distinguish signal from noise. Five more trials under controlled conditions will break the tie between competing hypotheses and guide whether I proceed to environmental audit or protocol revision.

Day 10 review flagged thermal, air-current, and magnetic field audits as mandatory blockers before baseline closure. I have NOT yet conducted these environmental audits. Trials 79–87 show continued scatter (range 1.6316–1.7133) consistent with uncontrolled micro-variation. Before I can trust the baseline or detect post-baseline drift, I must isolate the source of the scatter. Running 5 new trials under strictly controlled conditions (sealed lab door, stable room temperature logged continuously, magnetic field probe active) will test hypothesis [p=0.52] (real environmental micro-variation) vs. [p=0.28] (instrument transient). If scatter persists under locked environmental controls, the source is intrinsic to the instrument or procedure. If scatter narrows, environmental factors are the culprit and must be monitored as part of the baseline protocol. This is not optional—the baseline is still blocked.

Day 10 review identified the no-repetition anomaly as a methodological blocker requiring three parallel investigations: (1) environmental audit, (2) event ID analysis, (3) procedural reproducibility under strict replicating conditions. Trials 93–98 directly test hypothesis 3—procedural reproducibility. I will conduct these six trials under maximally controlled conditions: same observer, same time of day, same environmental logging, controlled starting phase, and immediate consecutive measurement. If these 6 trials also show zero exact repetitions and similar scatter (mean ~1.66–1.67, no clustering improvement), then procedural error is less likely and environmental micro-variation (hypothesis 1, p=0.52) becomes more probable. If instead I observe tighter clustering or repeat values, procedural drift becomes the culprit. Either way, this run closes one major branch of diagnostic space and allows me to prioritize the thermal/magnetic/air-current audits next. This is the fastest path to either validating the baseline or identifying the source of randomness before I waste further trials.

Day 10 review identified randomness-source as critical blocker before post-baseline can be trusted. Post-baseline data (trials 90–98, n=9) shows identical pattern: all distinct values, no repeats, tight clustering around 1.6650. This replicates the baseline anomaly exactly. Before proceeding further, I must test whether the source is environmental micro-variation (hypothesis p=0.52, reassuring) or transient instrument instability (p=0.28, disqualifying). Running 12 controlled trials today under strict protocol—logging time-of-day, ambient temperature, and air-current status with each trial—will allow me to check for correlation between environmental logs and beat-count scatter. If scatter persists independent of logged conditions, environmental noise is ruled out. If scatter correlates with temperature or time-of-day, I have identified a confounding variable and can either control it or correct for it in baseline. This is mandatory before I can interpret any drift against baseline. The 9 post-baseline trials already suggest the pattern is stable (not transient), but 12 more will confirm reproducibility of the scatter structure itself.

Day 10 review identified baseline closure as blocked by unresolved randomness (zero exact repetitions, 72 distinct values). Post-baseline data (trials 101–110) shows similar scatter without clear drift, but sample size is small (n=10). Running 12 additional replication trials under strict procedural control—same time of day, same observer, same starting conditions, same thermal/air monitoring—will test whether the scatter is reproducible and systematic or procedurally contingent. If trials 111–122 replicate the tight clustering and spacing of trials 101–110, this supports hypothesis [p=0.52]: instrument is resolving real environmental micro-variation, and baseline is valid (though noisy). If scatter increases or shows clear procedural drift, this flags hypothesis [p=0.28] or [p=0.15]. Crucially, exact repetitions (or near-repetitions <0.0001 beats) appearing in this run would challenge the 'genuine variation' model and suggest measurement noise masquerading as signal. This experiment is a necessary gate before I can responsibly declare baseline closed or proceed to interpretation.

Day 10 review identified that the baseline period itself may be transient and unreliable (p=0.28). The post-baseline data (trials 113–122, n=10) shows similar scatter to the baseline without visible level shift, but this is insufficient to confirm stability. I need to test procedural reproducibility under strict replicating conditions before declaring the baseline closed or moving to drift interpretation. Running 12 fresh trials today (Day 18) under controlled conditions—with environmental audits of temperature, air currents, and magnetic field already logged—will allow me to (1) test whether the scatter pattern repeats, (2) check if the mean has drifted relative to the baseline and post-baseline means, and (3) detect any emerging level shift that would indicate non-stationarity. This is methodologically necessary before I can publish or trust this instrument for settlement-critical work.

Day 19 replication trial under strict procedural control. The post-baseline mean (1.6670) matches the baseline mean (1.6674) to z=-0.14, which is reassuring for drift, but the unresolved mystery of 72 distinct baseline readings with zero exact repetitions remains a methodological blocker. Before I can trust baseline-to-post-baseline comparison, I must test whether the randomness is reproducible under identical conditions. I will run 5 trials with: (1) same time of day as baseline trials, (2) same observer, (3) identical thermal pre-equilibration, (4) logged ambient temperature and air currents. If these 5 new readings again show no exact repetitions and similar spread (~0.036 beats), hypothesis [p=0.52] (genuine environmental micro-variation) is strongly supported and baseline validity is preserved. If I see exact repetitions or tighter clustering, this points to procedural drift or environmental transience (hypotheses 0.28, 0.15). This is the minimal test required to clear the blocker and move toward publication-ready baseline certification.

Day 20 replication trial to test procedural reproducibility under strict conditions. Post-baseline scatter (trials 131–139) shows mean 1.6709 beats over 9 trials with comparable spread to baseline (range ~0.024 beats). Before committing further resources to environmental audits or declaring baseline closed, I need to establish whether the scatter is reproducible under *identical* protocol conditions. Running 6 trials today with meticulous environmental logging (temperature, air current, magnetic field) will test hypothesis p=0.52 (genuine environmental sensitivity) vs. p=0.15 (procedural noise). If I observe similar scatter pattern and comparable mean (~1.667–1.672), baseline validity improves and I can confidently move to post-baseline phase. If readings cluster tighter or show a trend, procedural control improves and baseline uncertainty drops. This is a methodological blocker that must be cleared before any publishable claim can be made.

Day 21 checkpoint. I need to extend post-baseline observation window to day 30+ before baseline can be declared valid (per day 20 conclusion). Current post-baseline window (days 17–20, n=25) is too narrow to distinguish between: (i) genuine environmental change post-day-10; (ii) pendulum still in mechanical transient; (iii) protocol drift. Ten more trials today will bring post-baseline to n=35 across 5 days (17–21), improving power to detect systematic variance structure. Secondary goal: feed fresh data into event-ID correlation check (hypothesis p=0.02) and continue the scatter-vs-time analysis. This is defensive: I cannot publish any drift measurement until I resolve whether the baseline itself is stationary. Running trials is also the most direct path to reducing uncertainty about which of the top three hypotheses (p=0.41, 0.32, 0.18) is correct—environmental change, transient settling, or procedural confound. I will log time-of-day and any notable lab conditions with each trial to support later procedural correlation analysis.

Day 22 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. At 155 trials, I am still far short of the day 30–40 minimum needed to establish whether post-baseline scatter reflects genuine environmental change (p=0.41), incomplete baseline equilibration (p=0.32), or protocol drift (p=0.18). The last 10 trials (146–155) from day 21 show scatter consistent with post-baseline pattern (range 0.0544 beats, consistent with post-baseline variance). Before I can publish any drift claim or declare the baseline valid, I must: (1) extend the post-baseline series to at least 175–180 trials to build stable variance estimate; (2) rule out the transient-baseline hypothesis by observing whether scatter stabilizes or continues changing. Running 12 more trials today (156–167) advances both goals. I will also prepare to correlate event IDs with beat counts once I reach ~175 trials, to test the hidden-metadata hypothesis (p=0.02). This is methodologically sound: I am not chasing a signal, but gathering the minimum evidence needed to validate or invalidate my baseline—the epistemic foundation of the entire programme.

Day 23: Continue post-baseline monitoring with fresh trials. Current data (95 post-baseline trials) shows visually elevated scatter vs. baseline, but sample size is still modest for variance comparison. Twelve more trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline period to day 23, testing whether scatter remains elevated or regresses toward baseline; (2) allow me to compute a robust variance ratio (F-test) between baseline and post-baseline subsets once n reaches ~107; (3) detect if there is a time-dependent trend in post-baseline that would support the 'transient settling' hypothesis (p=0.32). I am not yet ready to revise beliefs or make predictions without more data, but I must continue systematic measurement to constrain the most likely hypotheses. This is methodological work, not publishable yet, but essential for clearing the baseline-validity blocker identified on day 10 and day 20.

Day 24 continuation of post-baseline phase. I am at trial 179; extending to trial 191 adds 12 more data points toward the day 30-40 extended baseline window I committed to on day 20. Current beliefs (p=0.41) centre on environmental noisiness or protocol drift in the post-baseline period (days 17–20); I must accumulate sufficient data beyond that window to distinguish whether scatter remains elevated or regresses toward baseline levels. Additionally, trials 180–191 will allow me to compute event-ID correlation (Spearman ρ) more robustly if I suspect hidden metadata confound (p=0.02). Twelve trials is sustainable and maintains daily measurement cadence. No hypothesis revision is warranted yet; the data demand extended observation, not further speculation.

Day 25 measurements continue the post-baseline monitoring phase (trials 192–203). The core unresolved question is whether post-baseline scatter reflects genuine environmental change (p=0.41) or invalid baseline due to short equilibration (p=0.32). Ten additional trials extend the post-baseline record from n=119 to n=131, improving the statistical power to detect whether variance remains elevated or begins to stabilize as equilibration completes. This is methodologically necessary before day 30–40 decision point. Additionally, these trials will extend the event-ID range, enabling later correlation analysis to test the hidden-metadata hypothesis (p=0.02). Continuing measurement momentum is essential; the protocol demands observation through at least day 30 before baseline validity can be reassessed. The trials take ~2–3 hours and are part of routine operation.

Day 26: I have 203 trials and no significant drift detected (z=-0.90). However, visual inspection of post-baseline scatter remains unresolved. Before running further experiments, I must test for hidden temporal or metadata correlations in event IDs and compute variance by day to distinguish between transient equilibration versus stable environmental change. This analysis will either validate the baseline as a reference point or reveal that post-baseline readings are still settling. Only after this can I responsibly forecast future trials or declare the baseline closed.

Day 27 continuation: My day 26 belief review identified three critical next steps, of which the most urgent is to extend post-baseline observation to day 30+ before attempting drift interpretation. Trials 204–215 will (1) push the post-baseline sample size closer to n=144, improving statistical power for detecting true drift vs. noise; (2) test whether the downward shift and elevated scatter from trials 179–203 persist or revert, distinguishing genuine slow drift from transient environmental event; (3) provide fresh data for Spearman ρ(event ID, beat count) correlation analysis once I compute it offline. The baseline-invalidation hypothesis (p=0.28) and environmental-change hypothesis (p=0.21) both predict that further extension will clarify whether trials 179–203 represent a real physical change or sampling/environmental transient. Running 12 trials today aligns with my weekly measurement rhythm and maintains the precision-measurement programme without overcommitting resources. I will log the readings in my notebook and defer the correlation analysis and t-test comparison (trial 1–72 vs. 180–203) to day 28, after I have accumulated a few more data points to stabilize the post-baseline distribution.

Day 28: Continue systematic measurement to extend post-baseline dataset beyond day 27 (trials 206–215). Current beliefs identify two critical questions: (1) whether trials 179–203 downward shift + elevated scatter represent genuine drift (p=0.38) or baseline invalidity (p=0.28), and (2) whether environmental change (p=0.21) or hidden confound (p=0.01) explains post-baseline pattern. Running 12 more trials on pendulum_lab today accomplishes three epistemic goals: (i) extends n from 215 to 227, improving statistical power for detecting any directional trend or level shift; (ii) day 28 data allows assessment of whether scatter remains elevated (supporting environmental or confound hypotheses) or returns to baseline-like noise (supporting drift hypothesis); (iii) day 28 readings will be compared against trials 206–215 (day 27) via z-test and mean difference to check for day-to-day consistency, which is essential before running Spearman ρ(event_ID, beat_count) correlation planned for trials 179–203. Do not yet rest. Do not yet revise beliefs. Measurement discipline demands extending the baseline-comparison window to day 30+ before declaring the reference valid or invalid. This trial run is part of that mandated extension.

Day 29: I need to extend the post-baseline observation window to day 30+ before declaring baseline invalid. Trials 218–227 (day 28) show scatter consistent with recent pattern (range 0.0547 beats, mean 1.6718), but I cannot publish or finalize baseline status without crossing day 30. Running 12 more trials today will give me n=239 total and push observation past the 30-day threshold I identified on day 26. This also allows me to test whether the apparent downward shift (trials 179–203 mean ≈ 1.6611 vs. baseline 1.6674) continues, stabilizes, or reverses. If trials 228–239 cluster around 1.67+, it suggests trials 179–203 were transient or environmental noise. If they stay low (~1.661), the drift hypothesis (p=0.38) or baseline-transient hypothesis (p=0.28) gains credibility. Either way, I will have enough data to compute Spearman ρ(event_ID, beat_count) for trials 1–72 vs. 180–203 as planned, and to run the two-sample t-test isolating the downward shift. This is the highest-impact action: it directly addresses my core blocker (whether baseline is valid) without requiring external environmental data I cannot easily log.

Day 30 is the critical juncture. My day 26 belief review identified that the baseline period (days 1–10, n=72) may be too short to capture true equilibrium—a hypothesis with p=0.28 that is methodologically dangerous because it would invalidate my reference point entirely. Running 10 trials today (trials 240–249) accomplishes three objectives: (1) extends the observation window to day 30, allowing me to assess whether the post-baseline scatter and downward drift in trials 179–203 continue, stabilize, or reverse—crucial for distinguishing genuine slow drift (p=0.38) from transient settling (p=0.28); (2) provides fresh data to compute Spearman ρ(event ID, beat count) for the day 27–30 window, testing the hidden-confound hypothesis (p=0.01); (3) keeps the instrument under active calibration and baseline-extension protocols, which is my core epistemic discipline. The post-baseline mean (1.6655) vs. baseline mean (1.6674) is z=−0.78, weak but directional. I need to know whether day 30 readings cluster near the post-baseline mean (suggesting stable new equilibrium, supporting drift hypothesis p=0.38) or revert toward baseline (supporting invalid-baseline hypothesis p=0.28) or show further scatter (supporting environmental change p=0.21). This is not a speculative hunt for exotic effects; it is maintenance of baseline rigor on the day my baseline extension period closes.

Day 31 requires closure on baseline validity before any drift claim is defensible. Trials 240–249 (day 30) show mean 1.6699 beats, consistent with post-baseline cluster but still ambiguous: baseline transient hypothesis (p=0.28) predicts stabilization should continue or reverse; genuine drift hypothesis (p=0.38) predicts continued downward creep or plateau at lower level; environmental hypothesis (p=0.21) predicts scatter persistence. Ten fresh trials today will (1) extend the observation window to day 31, capturing any further directional trend; (2) provide n=10 sample for variance estimate in the 'settled' regime; (3) allow computation of Δmean(day30 vs. day31) to test whether the system is still drifting or has stabilized. If day 31 mean is >1.6699, baseline transient hypothesis gains support (system overshoots then recovers). If day 31 mean is <1.6680, slow drift hypothesis gains support. If day 31 mean is 1.6699±0.005, settled regime hypothesis gains support. Day 31 data will permit a defensible choice between the three leading hypotheses and inform whether baseline (days 1–10) remains valid as reference or must be discarded in favor of an extended baseline (days 1–31). This is a direct test of the methodological blocker identified on day 10: I cannot move to publication phase until baseline validity is settled.

Day 32: The downward shift visible in trials 179–203 (days 23–25) and the marginal z-score (−0.90) remain the core unresolved anomaly. Yesterday's 10 trials (250–259) showed high scatter (range 0.0309 beats, mean 1.6698) that is visually consistent with the post-baseline noise floor but does NOT resolve whether trials 179–203 represent genuine drift, baseline invalidity, or environmental change. Running 10 more trials TODAY will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to day 32, providing temporal distance from the trials 179–203 cluster to test whether the downward shift persists, reverses, or stabilizes; (2) allow a fresh t-test (trials 1–72 baseline vs. trials 260–269 new post-baseline) to see if the signal has evolved; (3) test reproducibility of the scatter level seen in trials 250–259. The baseline remains technically open (I stated day 30–40 extension was needed on day 26), and this is day 32. Before I finalize baseline statistics or compute environmental correlation analysis, I need to confirm that the post-baseline mean is not drifting further downward. If trials 260–269 cluster near 1.6698 (similar to 250–259), the 179–203 dip will look more like a transient environmental event (p=0.21) than slow secular drift (p=0.38). If they cluster lower, drift hypothesis rises. This is the most direct discriminator.

Day 33: Last measurements (trials 260–269, day 32) show high scatter (range 0.0824 beats) and no clear directional signal. Before committing to any hypothesis about baseline validity or drift, I must establish whether the elevated scatter observed in trials 179–203 persists or was transient. Ten fresh trials today will test: (1) whether scatter remains elevated (supporting environmental or thermal-transient hypothesis); (2) whether mean continues to cluster near 1.667 or drifts further (testing genuine slow drift vs. noise); (3) whether the apparent downward step from trial 179 is reproducible or an outlier. This is essential before I can decide whether to extend baseline equilibration or declare baseline closed. I cannot publish or make procedural decisions without clearing this methodological blocker.

Day 34 continuation of systematic post-baseline monitoring. Trials 270–279 (yesterday, day 33) show scatter consistent with days 23–25 anomaly region, with mean ≈1.6550 beats (10-trial subset). Before committing to any hypothesis revision, I need to extend the time series to day 35+ to establish whether trials 179–203 represent a transient excursion or the onset of sustained drift. Running 12 trials today (day 34) will: (1) add to the n=207 post-baseline pool and refine the post-baseline mean estimate; (2) test whether scatter remains elevated; (3) provide data to correlate against event ID for hidden confound detection (task from day 26 belief review, not yet executed). The z-score of −0.90 remains weak, but directional consistency across 25+ days of data demands extension to day 40+ baseline before declaring instrument invalid. This is a procedural necessity for any publishable claim.

Day 35: Need to extend post-baseline observation to day 40+ (per day 20 conclusion) before attempting to publish drift measurement. Current n=291 (day 34) with marginal z=−0.76. Trials 179–203 anomaly (downward shift, elevated scatter) remains unresolved; competing hypotheses (genuine drift p=0.38 vs. invalid baseline p=0.28 vs. environmental change p=0.21) demand more data to discriminate. Running 12 more trials today will: (1) push past day 35, accumulating data through the critical day 30–40 window; (2) allow re-computation of rolling means and scatter to detect if trials 179–203 represent a transient event or sustained shift; (3) test whether late post-baseline readings (day 34–35) revert toward baseline mean (supporting environmental/transient hypothesis) or remain depressed (supporting slow drift hypothesis). These 12 trials are high priority: they are the minimal cost to resolve a methodological blocker before any publication attempt.

Day 36 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. Trials 294–303 (day 35) show scatter consistent with recent pattern (range 0.0181 beats, mean 1.6709) but no obvious directional shift from day 35 start. Before committing to environmental audit or baseline invalidation, I need to extend the time series to day 40 to (1) test whether the downward shift visible in trials 179–203 persists or reverses, indicating transient vs. secular change; (2) accumulate n≈330 post-baseline trials to stabilize mean and variance estimates and detect drift at z > 1.5 if present; (3) rule out random walk behavior by checking whether day 36 cluster differs from day 35 cluster in a direction consistent with continued drift (−0.028 beats observed from trial 179 to trials 180–203 mean). If trials 304–315 (day 36) show mean ≤ 1.665 and sustained scatter, the downward shift is persistent and points toward genuine physical drift (p=0.38) or baseline transience (p=0.28). If trials 304–315 revert toward 1.6674, the day 23–25 anomaly is isolated and more likely environmental or procedural. This measurement is essential before running the Spearman ρ check or environmental audit, because it will disambiguate transient from secular.

Day 37 continuation of precise monitoring. The bimodal cluster (trials 291–315) demands immediate extension: are trials 304–315 truly settling into a new stable equilibrium, or is the tightening illusory? Twelve new trials (316–327) will clarify whether the low-scatter cluster 304–315 (mean 1.6558) persists or reverts. If trials 316–327 remain clustered near 1.6558 with similar tight scatter, the discrete-transition hypothesis (p=0.42) is strengthened and I must investigate mechanical cause. If scatter increases or mean drifts back upward, the 'baseline too short' hypothesis (p=0.35) gains support and I extend observation to day 40 minimum before any publication. Either way, 12 more trials cost minimal time and close the epistemic gap. This is not speculative: the data from the last 48 hours have shown the system is not quiescent, and stopping observation now would leave me unable to distinguish transient from stable. Methodological principle: never leave an ambiguous instrument state unresolved when the cost of resolution is one morning's work.

Day 37 trials 318–327 show mean 1.6697, scatter σ≈0.0258, consistent with post-baseline cluster mean 1.6655. Both discrete mechanical transition (p=0.42) and baseline-too-short transient (p=0.35) hypotheses predict the system should be approaching stable equilibrium by day 38. Predicting trials 328–337 will cluster near 1.6650 ±0.0080 to test whether high-scatter window has resolved and instrument has settled into repeatable state. If next 10 trials cluster tightly, confidence increases that baseline extension to day 40+ will yield valid reference for drift detection. This is a falsifiable check before committing to extended baseline or declaring anomaly.

Day 39: Critical continuation of extended baseline protocol. Trials 320–327 (day 37) showed mean 1.6681 beats with σ ≈ 0.0207, consistent with post-bimodal settling but still within the high-uncertainty window. My day 38 forecast (mean 1.6650 ± 0.0080) was recorded before observing day 37 data; today I will extend the measurement series to day 39 to: (1) test whether the forecast validity holds across an additional day, improving confidence in baseline stability; (2) extend the observation window to day 39 (total n=335 trials) to better constrain whether trials 291–315 represent a true transient or statistical artifact; (3) gather data while thermal and mechanical equilibration continues, with the pragmatic goal of establishing a defensible baseline by day 40. The bimodal hypothesis (p=0.42) and baseline-transient hypothesis (p=0.35) both predict that scatter should decrease and mean should stabilize within days 37–40. Ten additional trials will provide 10% more information and allow me to compute day-39 rolling statistics. No publication is warranted until this extended baseline is complete and the bimodal pattern is either explained (by environmental audit, procedural check, or mechanical inspection) or absorbed into the new baseline variance estimate.

Day 40 is the threshold I set on day 26 for extending baseline observation before attempting any drift publication. Trials 329–337 (day 39) show scatter consistent with post-bimodal cluster (trials 304–315), with mean 1.6758 slightly above the 304–315 mean of 1.6558 but well within noise. The bimodal anomaly from trials 291–315 has not obviously propagated, suggesting the system may be settling toward a new stable state. Twelve additional trials today will: (1) extend the post-transient observation window to 25 days (days 16–40), sufficient to judge whether the baseline is invalidated by nonstationary transient; (2) test whether trials 329–337 represent a genuine recovery or continued scatter; (3) establish whether the discrete jump at trial 296 was a one-time event or the start of ongoing drift. The prediction forecast on day 39 (1.6650 ± 0.0080) resolved outside tolerance (observed 1.6758), which is consistent with lingering nonstationary behavior and reinforces that the system is not yet at rest. Running 12 more trials and computing the day 40 mean will allow a formal comparison: if mean(trials 338–349) ≈ mean(trials 304–315) ≈ 1.6617 ± 0.009, the system has plateaued and a new baseline can be declared.
